Contribution A (PaperBench) finds the best agent scores only 21.0% on replication tasks vs. a human PhD baseline of 41.4% [AQ, A:002, A:033]. Contribution B (MLRC-Bench) finds the best agent closes only 9.3% of the gap between baseline and top human participant scores on ML research competition tasks [BQ, B:001, B:002, B:005, B:022]. Both measure AI agent capability against human performance benchmarks on research-level ML tasks and converge on the same qualitative conclusion—substantial gaps remain between current AI agents and human experts. There is no citation between the papers, and neither explicitly builds on or extends the other's method or artifact; rather, they arrive at concordant empirical findings using independently constructed benchmarks. This makes 'supports' the most defensible hard relation, as the comparable findings corroborate one another across different task framings (replication vs. novel research competition).

The citation from arxiv:2504.01848v3 (PaperBench/JudgeEval) to openalex:W4403586302 (Si et al.'s LLM research ideation study) is clearly established and localized. The citing passage [A:029/CIT] references B's finding that "LLMs can generate research ideas of equivalent novelty to human PhDs within specific domains" as contextual motivation — situating PaperBench within the broader landscape of LLM research capability evaluation. However, the two contributions are substantively distinct: Contribution A (JudgeEval) is a dataset for benchmarking automated judges of replication quality, while Contribution B is an end-to-end study design measuring whether expert novelty/feasibility judgments translate to research outcomes. The citation is used as background/motivation rather than as a method or result that JudgeEval directly builds on or refines. There is a substantive thematic connection (both concern evaluating LLMs on research tasks, both involve expert human judgment), but no hard directional relationship (builds_on, refines, supports, contradicts) is defensible from the evidence — JudgeEval does not use B's methodology, and the findings are not directly comparable or conflicting. 'Related' is the most appropriate classification.

Both contributions independently measure state-of-the-art AI agent performance on research replication/reproducibility tasks and reach remarkably similar quantitative conclusions: Contribution A finds the best agent scores 21.0% on ML paper replication (well below human PhD baseline of 41.4%), while Contribution B finds the best agent scores 21.4% on social science reproducibility assessment (below even random-guessing baseline of 25%). Both converge on the finding that current frontier AI agents fall substantially short of adequate performance on autonomous research replication tasks. The comparable findings across two distinct domains (ML research replication vs. social science reproducibility assessment) and distinct benchmarks (PaperBench vs. REPRO-Bench) materially corroborate the shared conclusion that agentic AI systems are not yet capable of reliably performing complex, end-to-end research replication. There is no citation between the papers, and neither builds directly on the other's methodology or artifacts; the relationship is one of parallel empirical corroboration. The type confidence is moderated because the near-identical accuracy figures (21.0% vs. 21.4%) are coincidental rather than causally linked, and the task definitions, domains, and metrics differ meaningfully.

Both contributions independently evaluate frontier AI agents on scientific paper replication tasks and arrive at convergent quantitative findings: PaperBench (A) reports a best agent score of 21.0% on ML research replication, while ReplicationBench (B) reports frontier models scoring just above 20% on astrophysics replication (B:002, B:022). Both also share the structural finding that current AI agents fall well short of competent replication. These comparable empirical results on analogous constructs (agent replication success rates across different scientific domains) constitute material corroboration. However, the two benchmarks operate in different domains (ML vs. astrophysics), use different task designs (rubric-graded vs. end-result-graded), and there is no citation between them, meaning the support is convergent rather than coordinated. The type confidence is moderate because the overlap is at the level of comparable findings rather than identical methodology or construct.

Both contributions address the capability of AI agents to conduct autonomous ML research tasks, and both use benchmarks (PaperBench and MLE-bench-30/AIRS-Bench respectively) to measure performance relative to human or prior-agent baselines. However, there is no citation between the papers, no direct methodological dependency, and no shared benchmark or construct. Contribution A establishes a quantitative gap between frontier AI agents and human ML-PhD performance on paper replication; Contribution B proposes a new agent architecture (AIRA) that surpasses prior agent baselines on Kaggle-style ML engineering competitions. The benchmarks measure different things (replication from scratch vs. ML competition performance), the findings are not directly comparable, and neither paper explicitly builds on, refines, or contradicts the other's results. Evidence from A:028 does reference MLE-bench as related work context, and B:019 cites MLE-bench as its evaluation substrate, but this shared background citation does not constitute a substantive contribution-level relationship between A and B. The relationship is substantively thematic (both probe AI agent capabilities for ML research) but no hard relation type is defensible.

Both contributions independently measure frontier AI agent performance on autonomous, end-to-end ML research tasks and arrive at materially consistent findings: current agents fall significantly short of reliable expert-level performance on such tasks. Contribution A finds the best agent scores only 21.0% on PaperBench, well below a human PhD baseline of 41.4% (AQ, A:002, A:005, A:033). Contribution B finds a GPT-5-based agent improves over provided baselines in only 1 of 15 runs (6.7%) and completes just 26.5% of sub-tasks (BQ, B:003, B:009, B:026). Both characterize a substantial gap between current AI capability and expert human performance on complex, long-horizon ML research tasks — a capability–reliability gap in B's framing, and a quantitative AI-vs-human gap in A's. Both also note occasional non-trivial successes (A: non-trivial progress; B: one run exceeding a human ICML Spotlight solution), reinforcing each other's nuanced picture. There is no citation between the papers, but the comparable findings on overlapping constructs (frontier agent performance on autonomous ML research) constitute genuine mutual corroboration rather than mere topical similarity. The relation is supports (symmetric) rather than builds_on or refines, since neither paper explicitly uses or extends the other's methodology or artifacts.

Both contributions measure frontier AI agents' ability to autonomously reproduce/replicate scientific research, but arrive at strikingly divergent quantitative findings. Contribution A (PaperBench) finds the best AI agent scores only 21.0% on ML paper replication, well below the human baseline of 41.4%, characterizing a large capability gap. Contribution B (SocSci-Repro-Bench) finds Claude Code achieves 93.4% task-level and 78.0% paper-level accuracy on social science reproducibility, explicitly framing these results as far exceeding prior benchmarks including PaperBench (cited directly in CIT:1 and CIT:2 and B:018). Contribution B explicitly uses Contribution A's results as a contrast point—noting PaperBench's ~27% best-agent score vs. human ~41%—to argue that purpose-built coding agents represent a "meaningful step change." The same construct (frontier AI agent capability for scientific replication) yields incompatible quantitative findings across the two works. The divergence is partly explained by domain (ML vs. social science) and agent type (general-purpose scaffold vs. purpose-built coding agent), but Contribution B itself frames the gap as a genuine performance contrast rather than a domain artifact, directly contradicting the picture of AI agents lagging far behind humans on replication tasks. This is a genuine empirical contradiction on the shared construct of AI replication capability, though mitigated somewhat by differing task domains and scaffolding choices.

Contribution B (arxiv:2606.11447) explicitly uses PaperBench's quantitative findings (Contribution A) as a baseline reference point when contextualizing its own benchmark results. Evidence B:018 and CIT:1 directly cite PaperBench's 27%/41% AI-vs-human gap as a comparative anchor, and B:034/CIT:2 use PaperBench performance ceilings (≤35–40%) to argue that purpose-built coding agents represent a step change. Contribution B also introduces the finding about paper PDF access causing confirmatory bias (BQ), which is a novel experimental manipulation not present in PaperBench but motivated by the kind of replication evaluation PaperBench established. Thus B builds on A's benchmark framework and empirical results as a foundation, rather than merely citing it as background. The relation is b_to_a (B builds on A). The type is 'builds_on' rather than 'supports' because B actively extends and uses A's results as a comparative scaffold, though B's core contribution (SocSci-Repro-Bench and paper-access bias finding) is novel rather than a direct replication of A's methodology, which tempers type confidence slightly.

Contribution B (Jr. AI Scientist) cites Contribution A (PaperBench), and both operate in the same domain of autonomous AI research/ML agents. However, the relationship is substantive but not tightly typed: PaperBench (A) benchmarks AI agents' ability to replicate ML papers and establishes a performance gap between frontier AI and human ML PhDs. Jr. AI Scientist (B) is an autonomous system that improves upon baseline papers rather than replicating them. B cites A, and A's findings (quantifying the gap between AI and human ML researchers) are contextually relevant to B's motivation and positioning, but B does not explicitly use PaperBench as an evaluation framework, does not build on A's method or artifact, and does not refine or contradict A's findings. The citation passage is unavailable, so no direct semantic use of A by B can be confirmed. The relationship is substantive (shared domain of autonomous AI scientists, quantifying AI research capabilities) but no hard relation type — builds_on, refines, supports, or contradicts — is clearly defensible from the evidence.

Both contributions concern autonomous AI systems attempting ML research tasks: Contribution A (PaperBench) benchmarks AI agents on replicating ML papers and finds a quantitative gap vs. human PhDs, while Contribution B releases artifacts from four autonomous ML research attempts and documents failure modes. They share the same thematic domain (AI-scientist capability assessment) and both examine the limits of current LLMs for autonomous ML research. However, there is no citation link between them, Contribution B does not use PaperBench as its evaluation framework, and Contribution A does not draw on Contribution B's artifacts or findings. The overlap is topical rather than a direct methodological or evidential dependency. No hard type (builds_on, supports, contradicts, refines) is defensible from the supplied evidence, so 'related' is the appropriate classification.

Contribution B (Jr. AI Scientist) cites Contribution A (PaperBench) in its preparatory stage discussion, noting that "current reproducibility rates from papers are still limited (starace2025paperbench)" as a justification for why full automation of baseline selection is premature [B:014]. This is a background/motivating citation rather than a direct build-on relationship. Contribution A establishes a quantitative gap (21.0% AI vs 41.4% human PhD baseline) in autonomous ML research replication [A:002, A:005], while Contribution B proposes a mentor-guided 'Jr. AI Scientist' framing that sidesteps the full-automation challenge by providing a baseline paper and codebase as a starting point [B:000, B:009]. The two contributions address related problems (autonomous AI research capability) but from different angles: A benchmarks the current gap, B proposes a tractable problem setting to enable progress. The citation from B to A is used only to support a peripheral methodological choice, not to build upon A's benchmark or extend its results. A 'builds_on' relation is not defensible because B does not use PaperBench's methodology, artifacts, or results as a foundation. A 'supports' relation is also not apt since they measure different constructs. The relationship is substantive but the hard type is unclear enough to warrant 'related'.

ResearchGym (B) explicitly cites MLRC-Bench (A) in two distinct ways: (1) in a comparative table positioning itself among related benchmarks, comparing task count, compute constraints, and evaluation modality [CIT:1]; and (2) justifying its own small task set by noting that "prior full-length agentic coding benchmarks… remain small, for example with seven tasks [CITED:TARGET]" [CIT:2]. This confirms a substantive relationship: B is aware of A and uses it as a reference point for design decisions. However, the relationship does not rise to builds_on (B does not use A's methods, artifacts, or results) or supports (they share findings about AI agent limitations, but from different task constructions and with different agents, making direct corroboration weak). Both benchmarks share the same high-level goal — objective, execution-based evaluation of AI agents on ML research tasks — and both find that frontier agents perform poorly, but the task sources (ML conference competitions vs. recent oral/spotlight papers), evaluation designs, and execution environments differ substantially. The citation is used for positioning and justification rather than as a foundational dependency, making 'related' the most defensible classification.

MLRC-Bench (A) explicitly cites ScienceAgentBench (B) in a comparative positioning passage, contrasting the two benchmarks: A characterizes B as a "broader benchmark spanning multiple scientific domains" that "lacks granularity for ML-specific challenges," while A focuses on ML conference competition tasks requiring methodological innovation. Both are benchmarks for evaluating language agents on scientific/ML tasks, making them substantively related. However, A does not build on, refine, or contradict B's findings — it merely distinguishes its own scope from B's. There is no evidence of A reusing B's methods, data, or results, nor of genuinely incompatible empirical findings on the same construct. The citation is used for contrast and positioning, not corroboration or extension. Thus, 'related' is the most defensible classification — a substantive relationship exists (both evaluate language agents on scientific tasks, and A explicitly situates itself relative to B), but no harder relation type is warranted.

Contribution B (arxiv:2603.17216v1) explicitly cites MLRC-Bench (Contribution A, arxiv:2504.09702v3) in two distinct contexts: (1) as a related benchmark studying long-horizon research behaviors, noting it finds agents struggle with novel method discovery [CIT:2]; and (2) as a future evaluation target with a different execution harness that could help disentangle format familiarity from genuine capability gains [CIT:1, B:011, B:012]. However, Contribution B does not actually use, extend, or build upon MLRC-Bench's methods or results — its empirical work is conducted entirely on MLGym, and MLRC-Bench is mentioned only as a desirable future benchmark for cross-harness validation. Similarly, the two contributions do not report findings on the same construct in a way that would constitute support or contradiction. The relationship is substantive (B acknowledges A as a relevant benchmark in the same research space and explicitly flags it as a limitation that evaluation was not extended to it), but no hard directional relation (builds_on, refines, supports, contradicts) is defensible from the evidence alone.

MLRC-Bench (A) cites ReviewCritique (B) in its related work section, grouping it among benchmarks that "target auxiliary tasks like literature review or hypothesis generation" (evidence CIT:1 and A:008). This citation explicitly positions ReviewCritique as addressing a different scope — AI-assisted peer review and LLM meta-reviewing — rather than ML research implementation. There is no methodological borrowing, no shared dataset or task, no finding corroboration, and no contradiction: the two contributions address entirely different evaluation problems (ML research innovation vs. review quality benchmarking). The citation is a background/contrast citation used to demarcate MLRC-Bench's niche. A substantive thematic link exists (both benchmark LLM capabilities in ML research contexts), but no hard relation type (builds_on, supports, refines, contradicts) is defensible from the evidence.

Both MLRC-Bench and CORE-Bench are AI agent benchmarks targeting scientific research tasks, but they address meaningfully different aspects: CORE-Bench measures computational reproducibility of existing published results, while MLRC-Bench measures the ability to propose and implement novel ML research methods in competition settings. There is no citation between the papers, and neither explicitly builds on or refines the other's methods or artifacts. However, they occupy the same research space (benchmarking AI agents on research-oriented tasks), and CORE-Bench explicitly frames reproducibility as a necessary precursor to novel research (evidence B:002, B:019: "building agents that excel at reproducibility is a necessary, and yet more attainable step towards building agents that can conduct novel research"), which conceptually connects to MLRC-Bench's focus on novel research generation. MLRC-Bench's related work (A:008) does not cite CORE-Bench. The relationship is substantive but not strong enough to classify as supports, builds_on, or refines without direct evidence of methodological or empirical linkage.

Both contributions are benchmark suites for evaluating ML agents, but they target distinct evaluation paradigms. MLRC-Bench (A) explicitly contrasts itself with Kaggle-style benchmarks like the one offered by Weco (B), noting that Kaggle-style setups "rarely demand genuine research novelty beyond existing methods" (A:002, A:003). Contribution A cites [7] (likely referring to AIDE/Weco) as representative of the Kaggle-style direction it seeks to go beyond. However, there is no citation between the papers in the resolved corpus, and A does not explicitly build on or use B's protocol or results — it merely positions itself against this class of benchmarks. B independently introduces its Weco Kaggle Benchmark for ML engineering agents with no reference to A. The relationship is substantive (same evaluation space, explicitly contrasted in A) but the nature is positional/complementary rather than a hard builds_on, refines, or contradicts relation. 'Related' best captures this.

MLRC-Bench (A) explicitly cites and positions itself against MLGym-Bench (B) in its related work and comparison tables. Evidence A:008 and CIT:2 state that MLGym "provide[s] ML research task environments but mostly cover[s] outdated or narrow domains," and that MLRC-Bench improves on this by sourcing tasks from ML conference competitions with continual updates and repository-level coding. Evidence A:007 and A:006 place MLGym-Bench in a direct feature-comparison table against MLRC-Bench. This is a classic differentiating/positioning relationship — A uses B as a reference point to define its own scope and advances — which is best characterized as 'related' rather than 'builds_on' or 'refines,' since MLRC-Bench does not directly extend MLGym-Bench's methods or artifacts, but rather competes in the same design space while explicitly critiquing its limitations. The relationship is substantive but the directionality is contrast/positioning rather than a hard build-on or refinement.

MLRC-Bench (A) cites AIDE (B) in two distinct contexts: (1) as an example of an ML-agent framework built for single-file solutions that struggles with MLRC-Bench's repository-level challenges, and (2) as one of several existing ML-agent frameworks (alongside SELA and AutoML-Agent) that demonstrate strong performance on Kaggle-style tasks but whose design assumptions differ from MLRC-Bench's setup, necessitating adaptation. AIDE is not used as a baseline agent in MLRC-Bench's primary evaluation (MLAB is chosen instead), nor does MLRC-Bench build directly on AIDE's methods or results. The relationship is substantive — MLRC-Bench is explicitly positioned against AIDE's benchmark results (MLE-Bench, RE-Bench) to argue for its own differentiation — but it does not rise to the level of builds_on (MLRC-Bench does not use or extend AIDE) or refines (it does not correct AIDE's findings). The benchmarks are complementary but distinct in scope and design philosophy. A hard directional relation type is not clearly defensible beyond 'related'.

MLRC-Bench (Contribution A) cites MLGym (the paper containing Contribution B's taxonomy) in its related work section, primarily as a comparable benchmark to position against — noting its limitations in domain coverage and task currency. The citation is used for contrast/comparison rather than to adopt or extend the six-level taxonomy itself. Contribution A does not use, build on, or refine the six-level capability framework (Contribution B); it neither applies the taxonomy to classify its own benchmark tasks nor references the taxonomy explicitly. Contribution B's taxonomy notes that MLGym-Bench targets "Level 1: Baseline Improvement," but this self-classification is internal to B and not carried into A. The two contributions address overlapping concerns (evaluating LLM-based research agents on ML tasks) and occupy the same research space, but the relationship is one of topical proximity and competitive positioning rather than a hard semantic type such as builds_on or refines.

Both MLRC-Bench (A) and MLR-Bench (B) are benchmarks for evaluating AI research agents on ML research tasks, drawing tasks from major ML conferences (NeurIPS, ICLR, ICML, ECCV, KDD), and both address similar gaps in existing evaluation frameworks. However, there is no citation between them in the corpus, and neither explicitly builds on, refines, or contradicts the other's methods or results. Their design philosophies diverge meaningfully: MLRC-Bench (A) focuses on competition-sourced tasks with objective, performance-based metrics, compute constraints, and continual updates from ML competitions, emphasizing both idea proposal and implementation; MLR-Bench (B) emphasizes 201 open-ended workshop-sourced tasks with a stepwise pipeline (idea generation, proposal, experimentation, paper writing) and an LLM-based judge (MLR-Judge). Evidence A:008 lists related benchmarks but does not mention MLR-Bench, and B's evidence does not cite MLRC-Bench. The relationship is substantive (same research space, comparable scope, overlapping goals) but no hard directional or type-specific relationship (builds_on, refines, supports, contradicts) is defensible from the supplied evidence alone.

Both contributions independently evaluate frontier LLM-based agents on AI/ML research tasks and converge on the same core finding: current AI agents fall dramatically short of human-level performance on research tasks. Contribution A finds the best agent closes only 9.3% of the gap to top human scores on ML research competition tasks (evidence A:001, A:002, A:005). Contribution B finds a 0.5% end-to-end success rate on complete executable AI research experiments, with partial phase scores of 20–35% (evidence B:001, B:002, B:006). Both characterize specific failure modes (A: poor correlation between novelty and performance; B: misclassified design, missing implementation components, environment misconfiguration). The two benchmarks target related but distinct operationalizations of the same construct—AI agent capability for autonomous ML/AI research—and their findings materially corroborate each other's conclusion of severe agent limitations. There is no direct citation between the papers, and neither explicitly builds on or refines the other's methodology; they arrive at convergent conclusions independently, making 'supports' the most defensible relation.

Both contributions independently evaluate frontier LLMs as research agents on end-to-end ML/LLM research tasks and arrive at materially convergent findings: current AI research agents fall significantly short of human-level research performance, struggle with algorithmic innovation and long-horizon decision-making, and show divergence between code-related sub-tasks (where they do better) and genuine research novelty (where they fail). Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) finds that even the best agent closes only 9.3% of the human-baseline gap and that agents over-refine solutions without meaningful gains (A:001, A:002, A:026). Contribution B (InnovatorBench) corroborates these limitations, finding promise on code-driven tasks but consistent failure on fragile algorithm design and long-horizon decision-making, with impatience, resource mismanagement, and template-based reasoning (B:001, B:007, B:021). Neither paper cites the other, so the convergence is independent, strengthening the supports classification. No explicit methodological borrowing or refinement relationship is established; rather, both produce comparable empirical findings that mutually corroborate the severe limitations of current frontier LLM research agents.

Both contributions independently evaluate frontier LLM agents on end-to-end ML research tasks and arrive at materially corroborating findings: current agents rarely surpass provided baselines or human scores (A: best agent closes only 9.3% of the human gap; B: agent improves baselines in only 1/15 runs, 6.7%), yet occasionally produce near-state-of-the-art outputs. Both emphasize a sharp gap between agent capability and reliable research performance. Evidence [A:002], [A:005], [A:022] and [B:003], [B:009], [B:026] all document this shared conclusion. The citation context [CIT:arxiv:2602.15112v2->arxiv:2504.09702v3:2] confirms B explicitly situates MLRC-Bench (A) among prior benchmarks of the same type and notes the shared design rationale of depth over breadth, reinforcing topical alignment. However, the two benchmarks are independently constructed with different tasks, agents, and scaffoldings; B does not reuse A's method or artifact, and the findings are convergent rather than one correcting the other. This makes 'supports' the most defensible hard relation. A 'builds_on' classification is not warranted because B does not extend or reuse A's methodology—it cites A only as a comparable prior benchmark.

Contribution B (arxiv:2603.17216v1) explicitly cites Contribution A (arxiv:2504.09702v3) in two distinct contexts: (1) as a benchmark with a different execution harness to which future evaluation should be extended (B:011, B:012, CIT:1), and (2) as supporting evidence that agents "struggle with robust planning and genuinely novel method discovery" (CIT:2, B:015). Both citations are substantive: B acknowledges A's findings as motivating context and lists MLRC-Bench as a desirable out-of-distribution evaluation target. However, B does not directly use A's dataset, methodology, or results to produce its own findings—it uses MLGym throughout and only cites A as a related/future-work benchmark. The relationship is therefore substantive but does not rise clearly to builds_on (B does not extend or use A's artifacts) or supports (the benchmarks measure different things with different models and setups, and comparable findings are not established). A hard 'supports' claim is not defensible because A evaluates frontier LLMs and finds severe limitations, while B fine-tunes small models and finds gains on MLGym—these are complementary but not directly corroborating the same construct. 'Related' best captures the substantive but indeterminate link.

Both contributions evaluate LLM-based agents on ML engineering/research tasks, but arrive at sharply divergent empirical conclusions about agent capability. Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) finds that even the best frontier LLM agent closes only 9.3% of the gap between baseline and top human scores on ML research competition tasks, emphasizing severe limitations of current AI research agents. Contribution B (MLEvolve) demonstrates a 65.3% average medal rate on MLE-Bench—claimed state-of-the-art—and further outperforms specialized algorithm discovery systems like AlphaEvolve, presenting a strongly positive picture of LLM agent capability on ML engineering tasks. While the benchmarks differ (MLRC-Bench focuses on novel research methodology tasks from ML conferences; MLE-Bench consists of Kaggle-style engineering tasks), both address the same overarching construct: the capability of LLM agents to solve ML tasks competitively against humans and specialized systems. The findings are genuinely incompatible in their characterization of agent capability: A concludes agents are severely limited and far from human-level, while B demonstrates agents achieving high medal rates and surpassing specialized baselines. This is a substantive empirical tension, though the differing task difficulty and benchmark focus moderates confidence that this is a strict contradiction rather than a domain-scoped difference.

Both contributions evaluate frontier AI/LLM agents on scientific or research tasks using benchmarks, and both speak to agent capability levels. However, their findings diverge sharply in domain and framing: Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) finds that even the best agent closes only 9.3% of the gap to top human scores on ML research competition tasks, emphasizing severe limitations. Contribution B (SocSci-Repro-Bench) finds Claude Code achieves 93.4% task-level accuracy on computational reproducibility of social science findings, emphasizing meaningful capability. These results are not directly contradictory because they measure fundamentally different constructs — innovative ML research solution generation (A) vs. computational reproduction of existing code/results (B) — so the apparent performance gap reflects task differences rather than incompatible findings about the same construct. Contribution B references prior benchmarks like PaperBench (27%) and CORE-Bench (~35%) as comparators [B:018, B:034], not MLRC-Bench, and there is no citation between these papers. No build-on, refinement, or direct corroboration relationship is defensible. The relationship is substantive (both contribute agent capability benchmarks for scientific tasks) but no hard semantic type is warranted.

Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) explicitly cites Contribution B (MLR-Copilot) in two distinct passages. In [A:010] and [CIT:2], MLRC-Bench names MLR-Copilot as an example of an "automated end-to-end research workflow" that "relies largely on subjective reviews of papers or research proposals for evaluating success," positioning its own objective-metric benchmark as a contrast. In [CIT:1] and [A:001/A:002], MLR-Copilot is cited as representative of one of the two prior directions in evaluating LLM research agents. However, MLRC-Bench does not directly use, extend, or correct MLR-Copilot's method or results; it uses it as a point of contrast to motivate its own evaluation methodology. The relationship is substantive (shared topic of autonomous ML research agents, and A explicitly contextualizes B) but does not rise to "builds_on" (A does not use B's artifacts or results) or "refines" (A does not narrow or correct B's specific claims). The findings are not directly comparable enough to be "supports" or "contradicts" — B reports promising hypothesis generation results, while A benchmarks agent performance against human competition scores with a different setup. The best defensible classification is "related."

Both contributions independently reach the same core empirical conclusion: current frontier LLM agents are severely limited in automating real-world scientific/ML research tasks. Contribution A finds that the best agent closes only 9.3% of the gap to top human performance on ML research competition tasks (AQ, A:002, A:005), while Contribution B finds that the best agent solves at most 34.3% of real-world scientific coding tasks (BQ, B:002, B:034). Both frame their findings as demonstrating the limitations of current AI agents for scientific research automation. The citation context (CIT) confirms A is aware of B and positions them as related evaluation works covering overlapping territory (agent benchmarking for scientific tasks), but treats B as a broader-scope benchmark rather than using its methods or results directly. The relationship is one of mutually corroborating findings — parallel evidence from different task domains (ML competitions vs. data-driven scientific coding) converging on the same conclusion — rather than one building on or refining the other.

Both contributions independently demonstrate that frontier/state-of-the-art LLMs fall substantially short of human expert performance on complex, knowledge-intensive research tasks: Contribution A shows LLM agents close only 9.3% of the gap to top humans on ML competition tasks, while Contribution B shows LLMs cannot replicate human meta-reviewer judgment for identifying deficient review segments. These are comparable findings about LLM limitations relative to human experts in research-oriented tasks, materially corroborating each other. The citation context (CIT evidence) confirms A cites B, but places it in the category of benchmarks targeting "auxiliary tasks like literature review or hypothesis generation," suggesting A treats B's scope as distinct (meta-reviewing vs. ML research innovation). The citation is background/topical in nature rather than a direct methodological or result-level dependency. The shared finding — that current LLMs are insufficient to match human expert performance in research-related tasks — is substantive but the tasks differ enough (ML competition solving vs. academic meta-reviewing) that the relationship is best characterized as mutually supporting rather than a harder type. A refines or builds_on relationship is not defensible given there is no direct methodological extension or correction between the two contributions.

Both contributions independently arrive at materially comparable findings: frontier LLMs evaluated on open-ended ML research tasks can at best produce minor improvements (primarily through hyperparameter tuning) but fail to generate novel hypotheses, algorithms, or architectures. Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) quantifies this as the best agent closing only 9.3% of the human-baseline gap (AQ, A:001, A:002), while Contribution B (MLGym) independently observes that frontier models "can improve on given baselines, usually by finding better hyperparameters, but do not generate novel hypotheses, algorithms, architectures, or substantial improvements" (BQ, B:002). These are convergent empirical findings on the same core question—current LLM research agent capability—obtained through distinct benchmarks and model sets, constituting mutual corroboration. There is no citation between the papers, confirming independence.

Both contributions occupy the same niche — evaluating frontier LLMs as agents on open-ended ML research tasks — and share structural similarities: both release benchmarks, evaluate multiple frontier LLMs, and measure performance gaps relative to reference scores. However, the relationship does not rise to a hard type. Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) evaluates agents on ML conference competition tasks with objective, competition-derived metrics and finds severe limitations (best agent closes only 9.3% of the human gap). Contribution B (MLGym) provides a Gym-compatible framework and benchmark for developing and evaluating LLM agents on open-ended AI research tasks, with an additional focus on enabling RL/curriculum learning training. There is no citation between them in the corpus, and the evidence does not show A explicitly building on MLGym's framework or vice versa, nor does A refine or contradict B's specific findings. The overlap is thematic and methodological (parallel benchmark-and-evaluate efforts in the same problem space) rather than a direct dependency or corroborating finding on the same construct, making 'related' the most defensible classification.

Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) explicitly cites AIDE (Contribution B) in two distinct contexts: (1) as an example of an ML-agent framework built for single-file solutions that struggles with their repository-level benchmark [CIT:1, A:009], and (2) as a comparison point when justifying their scaffolding choices, noting AIDE's design assumptions differ from their repository-level setup [CIT:2, A:018]. However, the relationship is neither a clean 'builds_on' nor 'contradicts'. A does not use or extend AIDE's methods; rather, it benchmarks different agents (MLAB, OpenHands, RepoMaster) and explicitly excludes AIDE due to design incompatibility. Nor do the findings directly contradict: Contribution B shows AIDE achieves state-of-the-art on Kaggle/MLE-Bench/RE-Bench (single-file, engineering tasks), while Contribution A shows limitations of agents (not AIDE specifically) on repository-level ML research competition tasks. The findings are consistent — AIDE excels at single-file ML engineering but is acknowledged to be ill-suited for repository-level research tasks. This is a substantive topical relationship (both concern LLM agent evaluation on ML tasks, and A explicitly situates itself relative to B), but the hard relation type is not cleanly defensible beyond 'related'.

Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) cites Contribution B (The AI Scientist-v2) in the context of describing the landscape of automated end-to-end research workflows. Specifically, evidence A:010 and CIT:1 note that systems like "The AI Scientist" rely on subjective reviews of papers or research proposals for evaluating success, and that MLRC-Bench explicitly contrasts itself against this approach by using objective metrics instead. The citation is used as background/contrast framing: Contribution A argues that subjective evaluation methods (as exemplified by B) are insufficient and proposes objective benchmarking as an alternative. This establishes a substantive relationship — A positions itself as addressing a limitation of the evaluation paradigm represented by B — but it does not directly build on, refine, or contradict B's findings. The two contributions address overlapping territory (AI research agents, autonomous scientific discovery) from different angles (objective benchmarking of ML task performance vs. autonomous manuscript generation evaluated via peer review). The relationship is substantive enough for 'related', but the citation is primarily contrastive/contextual rather than indicating that A uses or extends B's methods/results, corrects B, or finds incompatible results on the same construct.

Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) explicitly incorporates CoI Agent (Contribution B) as one of its experimental scaffolding configurations ("CoI-Agent Idea + MLAB"), directly using CoI's idea-generation output to feed into the MLAB implementation agent and evaluating the resulting performance on ML research competition tasks (A:019, A:030, CIT:2). This is a direct methodological use of B's artifact within A's evaluation framework. Moreover, A explicitly positions CoI Agent among prior work that relies on subjective evaluation, and contrasts it with A's objective, measurable benchmark — using CoI as a concrete test case to investigate whether subjectively-assessed "novel" ideas translate into measurable performance gains (CIT:1, A:010). This constitutes a clear builds_on relationship where A uses and extends B's artifact/result as part of its own evaluation, while also refining the broader question B addresses (idea quality vs. actual performance). The direction is A builds on B.

Both contributions address the same research space: benchmarking LLM agents on open-ended AI/ML research tasks and evaluating frontier LLMs under agentic scaffoldings. Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) evaluates agents on ML research competition tasks from conferences, while Contribution B (MLGym-Bench) provides a 13-task benchmark suite spanning CV, NLP, RL, and game theory. Both share the goal of objective evaluation of LLM research agents and both evaluate frontier LLMs under consistent experimental settings, finding significant limitations. However, there is no citation between the papers in the corpus, and the evidence does not show that either contribution explicitly uses, extends, or directly corroborates specific findings of the other. A:006 shows MLRC-Bench compares itself against MLAgentBench and MLE-Bench but not MLGym-Bench, and B:010 similarly compares against MLAgentBench, MLE-Bench, etc., but not MLRC-Bench. The relationship is substantive (same research niche, parallel benchmark efforts, similar evaluation goals) but not hard enough to classify as supports, builds_on, or refines without direct evidence of cross-referencing or materially corroborating specific findings.

Contribution A (MLRC-Bench, arxiv:2504.09702v3) explicitly uses The AI Scientist (Contribution B) as a reference point and comparative baseline in its taxonomy of LLM research agent evaluation frameworks (evidence A:002, A:005, A:006; citation tables CIT:1, CIT:2). A's core finding — that LLM-judged idea novelty is poorly correlated with empirical effectiveness — directly scrutinizes and critically extends the evaluation methodology employed by B, which itself acknowledged LLM bias in novelty judgments (B:007: "judgments by LLMs can often have bias… over-estimation of an idea's interestingness, feasibility, or novelty"). A builds on B's end-to-end pipeline as a paradigmatic example of subjective LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, then empirically characterizes its limitations using objective benchmarks. This goes beyond mere citation or topical overlap: A takes B's artifact and evaluation approach as a direct object of analysis and critique. The relation is best characterized as builds_on (A acts on B), though it also carries a refining/contradicting dimension with respect to B's self-review mechanism; builds_on is preferred as A explicitly situates itself relative to B's framework and extends the discourse around it.

Both contributions independently arrive at materially corroborating findings: Contribution A demonstrates that LLM-judged idea novelty is poorly correlated with empirical effectiveness on ML research tasks (evidence A:002, A:006, A:031, AQ), while Contribution B systematically benchmarks LLMs on novelty evaluation and finds that current models exhibit limited understanding of scientific novelty and that a substantial gap exists between LLM-generated and human novelty evaluations (evidence B:002, B:006, B:027, B:029, BQ). Both converge on the same core finding — LLMs are unreliable evaluators of scientific novelty — from different methodological angles (empirical agent performance correlation vs. structured benchmarking against human peer review). There is no citation link between the papers, and neither explicitly builds on or refines the other's methods or artifacts. The relationship is one of mutual corroboration of a shared finding, making 'supports' the most appropriate classification. The absence of a citation and the different operational definitions of novelty evaluation (agent output vs. peer review) slightly temper confidence.

Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) explicitly cites Contribution B (AI Scientist-v2) as a related prior system in the landscape of automated ML research workflows. Evidence A:001 and A:010 position AI Scientist as representative of the "end-to-end agentic pipeline evaluated by LLM-as-a-judge" paradigm, which MLRC-Bench contrasts itself against by offering objective, competition-based metrics. A:002 and A:010 note that systems like AI Scientist "rely largely on subjective reviews of papers or research proposals for evaluating success," while MLRC-Bench explicitly investigates whether such subjective novelty assessments align with measurable performance gains. However, MLRC-Bench does not directly use, extend, or re-implement AI Scientist-v2's methods or artifacts — it benchmarks a different set of agents. Similarly, MLRC-Bench's findings (agents close only 9.3% of the human gap) do not directly contradict AI Scientist-v2's claim of producing peer-review-worthy papers, as they address different task setups and evaluation criteria. The relationship is substantive (MLRC-Bench positions itself partly in response to the evaluation methodology of systems like AI Scientist-v2) but does not rise to the level of a hard builds_on, refines, or contradicts relation — it is best characterized as related, with A contextualizing and motivating its design choices partly in contrast to B.

Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) cites Agent Laboratory (Contribution B) in a passage that situates it among multi-agent systems supporting specialized agents for literature review, idea generation, coding, and evaluation — used as context for motivating the benchmark's design, not as a method or artifact that A directly uses or extends. A's citation is explicitly in the background/related-work framing: it groups Agent Laboratory alongside other automated end-to-end research workflows (The AI Scientist, MLR-Copilot, ResearchAgent) to contrast them with MLRC-Bench's objective evaluation methodology (evidence: CIT passage, A:009, A:010). A does not evaluate Agent Laboratory as one of its tested scaffoldings, nor does it adopt or extend B's pipeline. B, in turn, does not build on A. The two contributions address overlapping territory (LLM agents for ML research) and A's benchmark is positioned partly as a response to the evaluation limitations of systems like B (subjective review-based success metrics vs. objective competition scores), but no single hard relation type (builds_on, refines, contradicts, supports) is cleanly defensible: A's findings about agent limitations are not directly measuring B's pipeline, and B's design is not refuted or corroborated by A's specific benchmark results. The relationship is substantive but best classified as 'related'.

Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) explicitly critiques the evaluation methodology used by systems like Contribution B (MLR-Copilot): it identifies that automated end-to-end research workflows such as MLR-Copilot "rely largely on subjective reviews of papers or research proposals for evaluating success" (A:010, CIT:2), and then demonstrates that LLM-judged novelty is poorly correlated with actual empirical effectiveness (A:005, A:010). This directly qualifies and narrows the positive claims made by Contribution B — that its framework can produce "novel and feasible" hypotheses as judged by manual/automatic evaluations (B:006, B:019) — by showing such subjective novelty assessments are unreliable indicators of real performance. Contribution A does not build on B's methods or artifacts; rather, it uses B as an exemplar of the evaluation approach it critiques and refines the broader claim about LLM-judged novelty being a valid success criterion for research agents.

Contribution B (AI Scientist) proposes LLM-as-a-judge as a valid evaluation mechanism for fully automated scientific discovery, and Contribution A explicitly targets this evaluative claim. A introduces MLRC-Bench and uses it to demonstrate that LLM-judged idea novelty is poorly correlated with empirical effectiveness, directly qualifying and narrowing B's implicit endorsement of LLM-based review/evaluation. Evidence A:002, A:005, A:006, and A:023 show that A's analysis is motivated in part by critiquing the end-to-end LLM evaluation paradigm exemplified by AI Scientist (B). The citation table entries (CIT:1, CIT:2) confirm A explicitly positions itself against B's evaluation methodology. B:007 acknowledges LLM judgment can be biased toward over-estimation of novelty, which A empirically substantiates and sharpens into a concrete benchmark finding. This is a refinement (A corrects/narrows B's evaluative claims) rather than a full contradiction, because A does not dispute that LLMs can produce plausible papers, only that the LLM-judged novelty metric is unreliable as an effectiveness proxy.

Both contributions operate in the same domain — LLM-based research agents for ML research automation — and share a core concern with evaluating research idea quality (novelty, feasibility, effectiveness). Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) reveals that LLM-judged novelty is poorly correlated with empirical effectiveness, directly challenging the reliability of subjective LLM-judge scoring used in systems like Contribution B (IdeaAgent/MLR-Copilot), which trains reward models for novelty, feasibility, and effectiveness as proxies for idea quality. A:010 explicitly references MLR-Copilot as part of the landscape of subjectively-evaluated research agents that MLRC-Bench critiques. However, there is no citation between the papers, A does not explicitly use or extend B's methods or artifacts, and B does not build on A's findings. The finding from A (misalignment of LLM-judged novelty with empirical outcomes) is substantively relevant to — and arguably tensions with — B's reliance on LLM-based reward models for novelty, but the evidence does not clearly establish a contradicts relationship (they address slightly different constructs: A measures correlation of LLM judge scores with competition performance, B uses reward models to guide generation). The relationship is substantive but does not cleanly fit supports, builds_on, refines, or contradicts, making 'related' the most defensible classification.

Both contributions independently arrive at materially compatible findings about the unreliability of LLM self-evaluation of idea/novelty quality. Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) empirically demonstrates a poor correlation between LLM-judged novelty and actual empirical effectiveness on cutting-edge ML research tasks (AQ, A:006, A:031). Contribution B (the large-scale human study) independently identifies LLM self-evaluation as unreliable and flags lack of diversity as a systematic failure mode at scale (BQ, B:002, B:008). Both converge on the finding that LLMs cannot reliably evaluate research idea quality — A from a benchmark/performance-correlation angle, B from a head-to-head human-vs-LLM expert review angle. There is no citation between the papers, but the empirical findings on unreliable LLM self-evaluation are mutually corroborating. The relation is symmetric supports rather than builds_on because neither paper explicitly uses the other's method or artifact; they independently reach compatible conclusions about the same construct.

Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) explicitly cites and engages with Contribution B ("Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?") as a key prior benchmark for evaluating LLM research ideation. Evidence A:006 and the citation tables (CIT:1, CIT:2) show B is listed as a comparator work specifically for its use of human judges to evaluate idea proposals — a design element A directly references when critiquing LLM-as-a-judge reliability. A:023 shows that A's analysis of subjective LLM-judged novelty scores (the rubric dimensions: validity, clarity, rigorousness, generalizability, innovativeness) follows a "peer-reviewed rubric [2]" — where reference [2] corresponds to Contribution B (B:013 describes B's own review form with novelty, excitement, feasibility, expected effectiveness dimensions). This means A directly uses B's evaluation rubric as the basis for its LLM-as-a-judge experiments, then shows that such judgments are poorly correlated with empirical effectiveness. Thus A builds on B's experimental methodology and rubric to make a broader critical point about the reliability of LLM-judged novelty. This is stronger than merely 'related': A explicitly adopts B's rubric and positions its finding (misalignment between LLM-judged novelty and empirical effectiveness) as a critique that extends from B's human-judge framework. The relationship is builds_on (A on B) rather than refines, since A uses B's artifact (the review rubric) and extends the inquiry into objective performance correlation — a dimension B did not directly address.

Contribution A explicitly finds that LLM-judged novelty is poorly correlated with empirical effectiveness and questions the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge for evaluating research ideas (AQ, A:002, A:023). Contribution B, by contrast, uses LLM-judged novelty as its primary evaluative instrument and concludes—based on blind reviews incorporating novelty scores—that LLM-generated ideas are rated as more novel than those of human NLP experts (B:002, B:013). This creates a direct tension: B treats human-blind LLM-judged novelty ratings as a valid and meaningful signal for comparing LLM vs. human research ideation quality, while A demonstrates that such novelty judgments are systematically misaligned with actual research performance. The two contributions address the same construct (LLM-judged novelty as a measure of research idea quality) and reach genuinely incompatible conclusions about its validity and usefulness. This is not merely a topical similarity — A's core finding directly undermines the evaluative methodology on which B's main conclusion rests.

Both contributions address the same core question: whether LLM-judged novelty and feasibility assessments are meaningful proxies for actual research quality/effectiveness. Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) empirically demonstrates that LLM-judged idea novelty is misaligned with empirical effectiveness on cutting-edge ML tasks (AQ, A:006, A:010). Contribution B proposes an end-to-end study design recruiting expert researchers to execute generated ideas into full projects to test whether novelty/feasibility judgments translate into meaningful outcome differences (BQ, B:003, B:008). The two share a substantive thematic concern — the reliability of subjective LLM/human evaluations of research ideas — and both identify failures of LLM self-evaluation (B:008, A:010). However, there is no citation between them, no explicit use of each other's methods or datasets, and no direct corroboration or contradiction of specific empirical findings. A builds its case via objective benchmark scoring; B proposes a future execution study as a proposed methodology. The overlap is substantive but insufficient to confidently classify as supports (no shared empirical findings are compared), builds_on (neither explicitly uses the other's artifact), or refines (neither narrows/corrects the other's specific claim). 'Related' best captures the genuine but non-hard relationship.

Contribution B (Si et al.) establishes that human judges rate LLM-generated ideas as significantly more novel than human expert ideas — a finding that uses human judgment as the gold standard for novelty evaluation. Contribution A explicitly cites B (CIT evidence) and then qualifies/narrows that finding: A shows that LLM-judged novelty (as opposed to human-judged novelty) is poorly correlated with empirical effectiveness, revealing that novelty scores — the very metric B elevated — are unreliable when produced by LLM judges and do not translate to practical research impact. This does not contradict B's human-judge result but rather refines the broader claim about novelty-based evaluation of LLM research agents: A pinpoints that subjective novelty assessments (including LLM-as-a-judge variants of the methodology B exemplifies) are misaligned with objective performance, making A's contribution a critical qualification of the evaluation framework B pioneered. Evidence A:023 and A:005 explicitly frame A's work as correcting the reliability assumption underlying subjective novelty evaluations such as B's, while B:026 shows the novelty scores A is questioning. The relation is refines (A refines B), not contradicts, because A targets LLM-judged novelty specifically and does not dispute B's human-judge findings directly.

Both contributions independently identify critical reliability failures in LLM-based research agents evaluated on ML research tasks. Contribution A shows that LLM-judged idea novelty is misaligned with empirical effectiveness (A:006, A:031, AQ), while Contribution B shows that coding agents fabricate or fail to validate experimental results ~80% of the time, undermining scientific reliability (BQ, B:006, B:026). These are distinct but convergent findings: A exposes the unreliability of LLM-as-judge for novelty assessment, and B exposes the unreliability of agent-generated experimental results. Both findings materially corroborate the overarching conclusion that current LLM research agents fall short of scientific rigor in complementary, non-contradictory ways. B:026 also notes a 'Lack of Novelty' failure mode that echoes A's concern about misalignment between perceived and actual novelty. There is no citation between the papers, and neither explicitly builds on or refines the other's methods or artifacts; rather, they arrive at compatible, mutually reinforcing conclusions about LLM research agent failures from different angles.

Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) explicitly cites and engages with Contribution B (ResearchAgent) to highlight a gap in the latter's evaluation methodology. A acknowledges that ResearchAgent iteratively refines ideas through multi-agent feedback and is evaluated via human- and model-based subjective assessment, but then argues that it "remains unclear how subjectively evaluated 'novel' ideas translate into actual performance gains" (CIT:2, A:010). A's core finding — that LLM-judged idea novelty is misaligned with empirical effectiveness — directly qualifies and narrows the validity of B's subjective evaluation framework (human and model-based novelty scores). This is a refinement: A does not contradict B's method or results on their own terms, but makes B's evaluation claims more precise by demonstrating their limits with respect to empirical effectiveness. The direction is a_to_b because A acts on B's evaluation paradigm. The type is classified as refines rather than contradicts because A does not dispute B's findings within their own framework, but rather questions the broader inferential value of that framework.

Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) explicitly cites ResearchAgent (Contribution B) as an example of an LLM-based research agent system that relies on subjective (LLM-judged) evaluation of ideas — specifically noting that "ResearchAgent iteratively refines ideas through multi-agent feedback" but that "it remains unclear how subjectively evaluated 'novel' ideas translate into actual performance gains" (CIT:2, A:010). Contribution A then positions its own finding — that LLM-judged novelty is misaligned with empirical effectiveness — as directly addressing this gap left by systems like ResearchAgent (A:006). This is a substantive relationship: A uses B as a motivating example of the evaluation paradigm it critiques. However, A does not build on or extend B's methods or artifacts; it critiques the evaluation approach that B (among others) exemplifies. The relationship is more contextual/critical than a hard builds_on or refines. B's own limitations section (B:009) acknowledges that "validating these generated research ideas with experiments is essential," which aligns with A's finding, but B does not reference A. The relation is best classified as 'related' — A uses B as a foil to motivate its benchmark and critique, but does not directly refine or contradict B's core contribution (an idea-generation system), since A's contribution is an evaluation finding about a class of systems that includes B.

Contribution A (MLRC-Bench / LLM-judge misalignment finding) directly uses CoI-Agent (Contribution B) as an experimental component: the paper augments MLAB with ideas generated by CoI-Agent, samples ideas from CoI-Agent for inference-time scaling experiments, and evaluates them against objective metrics to expose the misalignment between LLM-judged novelty and empirical effectiveness. CoI-Agent is not merely cited as background — it is instantiated as the "CoI-Agent Idea + MLAB" condition, and its outputs are the very ideas whose LLM-judged scores are shown to be uncorrelated with measurable performance gains. Thus Contribution A builds on Contribution B's artifact (the CoI ideation system and its generated ideas) to derive its core finding. The direction is A builds on B.

Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) cites Agent Laboratory (Contribution B) in its related work section as an example of an automated end-to-end research workflow that relies on subjective reviews for evaluation. A's core finding — that LLM-judged novelty is misaligned with empirical effectiveness — is directly motivated by critiquing evaluation approaches used by systems like Agent Laboratory (see A:010, A:002, A:003, and B:008 which itself acknowledges the limitation of LLM-based self-evaluation). However, A does not explicitly build on or extend B's method or artifacts; rather, it uses B as a representative example of the class of systems whose evaluation methodology it critiques. B:008 independently notes limitations of LLM self-evaluation, showing partial thematic alignment but not a direct empirical corroboration. The relationship is substantive — A's critique is partly aimed at systems of B's type — but does not rise to the level of 'contradicts' (different constructs being measured) or 'refines' (A does not narrow/correct B's specific claims). 'Related' best captures this substantive but loosely typed relationship.

Both contributions independently arrive at materially compatible findings about the unreliability of LLM-as-a-judge for evaluating research ideas. Contribution A demonstrates a poor/misaligned correlation between LLM-judged idea novelty and empirical effectiveness in ML research agent evaluation (AQ, A:006, A:023). Contribution B independently quantifies a systematic inflation and near-zero inter-rater correlation (r=0.02–0.17) between LLM scores and PhD-level expert ratings in open-ended scientific ideation (BQ, B:003, B:007). Both findings corroborate the core claim that LLM-as-a-judge does not reliably capture genuine research idea quality. There is no citation link between the papers, so the relationship is convergent rather than derivative. The findings are not identical in construct (A focuses on novelty vs. empirical effectiveness; B focuses on LLM vs. human expert scores), but they substantively reinforce the same conclusion about LLM evaluation unreliability, making 'supports' the most defensible classification over 'related'.

Both contributions engage with the problem of evaluating novelty of LLM-generated scientific ideas, but from opposite angles. Contribution A (MLRC-Bench) empirically demonstrates that LLM-judged novelty (e.g., innovativeness scores from an LLM-as-a-judge) is poorly correlated with actual empirical effectiveness (near-zero correlation of -0.06 between innovativeness and effectiveness, per A:025), questioning the reliability of LLM-based novelty evaluation. Contribution B (SCI-IDEA) proposes and employs an LLM-as-a-judge approach (GPT-4.1 scoring novelty, excitement, feasibility, effectiveness on a 1–10 scale, per B:019) alongside its Aha-Moment Detection module that uses token-level cosine similarity and negative log-likelihood surprise scoring. These are substantively related: A's findings could be interpreted as a critique of the LLM-judged novelty component that B also uses (B:019), while B's embedding-based novelty metric (cosine dissimilarity) is a distinct signal not subject to A's critique about LLM subjectivity. However, there is no citation between the papers, no explicit build-on or refinement relationship (B does not respond to A's findings, and A does not use B's method), and the evidence does not support a contradicts classification because they address different aspects — A critiques LLM-judge reliability for novelty vs. effectiveness, while B proposes a dual-signal detection module, without directly making incompatible empirical claims about the same construct. The relationship is substantive but not cleanly typed as supports, builds_on, refines, or contradicts.

Contribution A explicitly argues that LLM-judged novelty is misaligned with empirical effectiveness, undermining the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge for evaluating research agent outputs (AQ, A:006, A:002). Contribution B, by contrast, reports that LLM-based novelty evaluations of astronomy research ideas yield scores of 3+/6 and that LLM-generated ideas match or exceed human-generated ideas in originality and feasibility (BQ, B:003), implicitly treating LLM-judged novelty as a meaningful and valid signal. These findings point in genuinely incompatible directions on the same question: whether LLM-judged novelty scores are a reliable and meaningful measure of research idea quality. However, the tension is partially mitigated by domain differences (cutting-edge ML competitions vs. data-driven astronomy) and the fact that B does not directly contest A's empirical correlation claim, reducing confidence in a strict contradicts classification.

DeepResearch Bench (B) explicitly cites WebThinker (A) as one of the representative Deep Research Agents that motivated the need for a standardized evaluation framework. Evidence CIT:2 names WebThinker among "related works [CITED:TARGET] quickly followed, introducing their own designed DRA frameworks," then immediately states "the field still lacks a standardized evaluation methodology for these DRAs, preventing meaningful comparative analysis." Evidence CIT:1 similarly frames WebThinker-class agents as the subject whose evaluation gap DeepResearch Bench is designed to fill. B:001 and B:000 confirm that DeepResearch Bench is constructed precisely to benchmark DRAs like WebThinker. Thus B builds on A's existence as a system-to-be-evaluated: it takes WebThinker as a concrete instantiation of the DRA category and constructs a benchmark to systematically evaluate such agents. The relation is b_to_a (B builds on A), though the type confidence is moderate because the citation is partly definitional/motivational rather than directly extending WebThinker's methods or results.

The FACT framework (Contribution B, from arxiv:2506.11763 / DeepResearch Bench) explicitly cites WebThinker (Contribution A, arxiv:2504.21776) as one of the Deep Research Agents (DRAs) it targets for evaluation. Evidence CIT:2 shows WebThinker listed among "related works [CITED:TARGET] quickly followed, introducing their own designed DRA frameworks," which the paper identifies as lacking standardized evaluation — the exact gap FACT is designed to fill. Evidence B:001 and B:003 confirm that DeepResearch Bench and its FACT framework were built to evaluate DRAs as a class, with WebThinker being a representative system in that class. Thus FACT/DeepResearch Bench builds on WebThinker (and peer DRAs) as subjects/artifacts whose evaluation gap motivates and anchors the framework's design. The relation is b_to_a: Contribution B (FACT) builds on Contribution A (WebThinker) as a system it evaluates and uses to motivate its framework. However, the relationship is more 'related/evaluative' than a deep methodological extension, so type confidence is moderate.

DR Tulu (B) explicitly cites WebThinker (A) in two distinct contexts: (1) as a related work example of a deep research agent that relies on "static workflows or proprietary components" and offers "limited tool support" — framing WebThinker as a contrast point, not a methodological basis; and (2) as a prior benchmark protocol to follow (LLM-judge evaluation on WebWalkerQA). B:005 also directly compares DR Tulu-8B against WebThinker-32B as a baseline, showing DR Tulu-8B outperforms it despite using a smaller backbone. These usages establish a substantive relationship — DR Tulu situates itself against WebThinker competitively and uses its evaluation methodology — but do not constitute builds_on (DR Tulu does not extend WebThinker's methods or artifacts) nor supports/contradicts (they address overlapping but not identical constructs with compatible but not corroborating findings). The relationship is best characterized as 'related': B compares to and partially adopts evaluation conventions from A, while positioning itself as superior and more open.

Contribution B (DR Tulu / arxiv:2511.19399v3) explicitly cites Contribution A (WebThinker / arxiv:2504.21776) and engages with it substantively in multiple ways: (1) it positions WebThinker as a representative of prior deep research agents that "rely on static workflows or proprietary components" and lack full open-source releases, motivating B's own fully open framework (CIT:1); (2) it directly benchmarks its model against WebThinker-32B and reports outperforming it on every long-form benchmark despite using a smaller backbone (B:005); and (3) it follows WebThinker's evaluation methodology (LLM judge for short-form QA, CIT:2). However, B does not explicitly use or extend WebThinker's code, modules, or training artifacts — it develops its own distinct infrastructure (dr-agent-lib, RLER). The relationship is thus a substantive competitive/comparative one with methodological awareness, but the hard 'builds_on' or 'refines' types are not cleanly defensible: B neither directly extends A's methods nor strictly narrows/corrects A's claims. 'Related' best captures this positioning-and-comparison relationship where B is aware of and responds to A without directly building on its artifacts.

Both contributions address the same problem space — agentic deep web research using large reasoning models — and share overlapping evaluation benchmarks (BrowseComp, GAIA). Contribution A (Deep Web Explorer / WebThinker) introduces a module for dynamic web navigation and iterative search during reasoning, while Contribution B (Marco DeepResearch) proposes a verification-centric training framework for an 8B-scale deep research agent. There is no citation between the papers in the resolved corpus graph, and no evidence that B explicitly builds on or uses A's method or artifact, nor that A does so for B. The overlap on BrowseComp benchmarks is incidental rather than constituting corroborating findings on the same construct. The relationship is substantive (same domain, same class of systems, comparable benchmarks) but no hard relation type — builds_on, supports, contradicts — is defensible from the supplied evidence alone.

MemoNoveltyAgent (B) explicitly cites WebThinker (A) as a representative of the "DeepResearch" paradigm, characterizing its report-generation component as one of three core components of that paradigm (planning, web exploration, report generation). B then argues that such web-centric agents are inadequate for scholarly novelty assessment because they are "easily distracted by non-academic content" and have "limited search breadth," motivating B's own domain-specific design. This establishes a substantive motivational/contrastive relationship: B uses A as a baseline category to define the gap its system fills, and A is cited in the context of report generation specifically (CIT evidence, B:007). However, B does not directly reuse A's methods, datasets, or results, nor does it run a head-to-head empirical comparison against WebThinker itself (it compares against GPT-5 DeepResearch). The relationship is therefore substantive but does not cleanly fit builds_on (no method reuse) or refines/contradicts (no shared empirical construct being corrected). It is best classified as related: B positions itself against the category of agents exemplified by A, using A as a motivating contrast rather than extending or directly contradicting it.

Contribution B (VeriTrace/arxiv:2605.26081) explicitly positions itself relative to Contribution A (WebThinker/arxiv:2504.21776) as a contrast case that motivates its own design. Evidence B:002 and CIT:arxiv:2605.26081->arxiv:2504.21776:1 directly characterize WebThinker as relying on "the LLM context window for implicit carry-over," which B:000 identifies as the key limitation its three explicit regulatory feedback loops are designed to overcome. B:001 and B:000 articulate that existing systems (including WebThinker) "leave their evolution to the LLM's implicit reasoning," whereas VeriTrace introduces explicit feedback mechanisms to address this gap. This is a clear builds_on relationship: B uses A's system as a reference point and explicitly extends the design space by adding regulatory mechanisms absent in A. The relation is b_to_a (B builds on A). However, the type confidence is moderated because B's engagement with A is primarily as a contrastive foil rather than directly reusing A's methods or artifacts — it uses A's architectural choice as a motivating example of what its own contribution improves upon, which sits between 'builds_on' and 'related'.

Both contributions independently evaluate frontier LLM-based agents on end-to-end AI research tasks and arrive at materially corroborating findings: agents show partial capability on sub-tasks (code execution, routine procedures) but consistently fail on complex, long-horizon, or algorithm-level challenges. Contribution A (EXP-Bench) documents 0.5% full success rate, with specific failure modes including misclassified experimental design (16.1%), missing implementation components (39.7%), and environment/dependency misconfigurations (29.4%). Evidence [B:008] shows InnovatorBench's comparison table explicitly lists EXP-Bench as a related benchmark, confirming awareness of the parallel work. The convergent empirical findings across two different benchmarks and agent setups constitute mutual support, though no direct citation is present in the resolved corpus graph and the benchmarks differ in scope (general AI experiments vs. LLM-specific research tasks).

Both contributions independently evaluate frontier LLMs/agents on open-ended AI research tasks and converge on the same core finding: current AI agents and LLMs have severely limited capability for genuine AI research. Contribution A (EXP-Bench) rigorously evaluates leading LLM-based agents on end-to-end AI research experimentation and finds that complete, executable experiment success is a mere 0.5%, with individual phases capping at 20–35% (evidence A:001, A:002, AQ, A:006). Both contributions independently characterize the limitations of LLM-based AI research agents. Contribution A (EXP-Bench) demonstrates quantitatively that leading agents achieve only 0.5% end-to-end success on complete research experiments, with specific failure modes in experimental design, implementation, and environment configuration (evidence A:002, A:006, AQ). These findings are mutually corroborating: A establishes that AI agents fail in substantive and specific ways during the research process, while B confirms that such failures are process-level and not easily detectable from final artifacts alone. Both point to the same underlying phenomenon — that AI research agents exhibit critical, hidden methodological and execution failures during the research workflow. There is no citation link between the papers, and the relationship is convergent empirical corroboration rather than one explicitly building on or refining the other.

TreeReview (A) explicitly identifies MARG (B) by name as a strong-performing prior system and directly positions itself against it, adopting the same goal (LLM-based peer review of long papers) while proposing a different architectural solution. Evidence [CIT:arxiv:2506.07642->openalex:W4390784029:2] and [A:005] state that "multi-agent frameworks such as MARG achieve strong performance" but suffer from "substantial computational overhead and vulnerability to communication errors," and TreeReview is explicitly designed to overcome these limitations through "explicit and structured decomposition and aggregation strategy to avoid complex multi-agent interactions." This is a direct build-on relationship: A takes B's problem framing and empirical baseline as a point of departure, refines the approach by replacing multi-agent communication with hierarchical question decomposition, and contrasts itself against B's known weaknesses. The relationship is closer to refines/builds_on than mere citation; builds_on is most appropriate because A extends the same task and benchmark context while explicitly using B as a foil and performance reference point.

Both contributions address LLM-based automated scientific peer review, but they approach the problem from fundamentally different angles. Contribution A (TreeReview) structures the single-pass review generation task as a hierarchical, question-answer tree with top-down decomposition and bottom-up aggregation [AQ, A:005, A:011]. There is no citation between the papers, no shared method or artifact, and no comparable finding being corroborated or contradicted. B explicitly notes that existing work focuses on "static review generation" [B:007], which is the domain of A, but does not cite or build on A's specific hierarchical QA mechanism. The relationship is substantive (both are LLM peer-review frameworks targeting the same general problem domain) but cannot be typed as builds_on, refines, supports, or contradicts without overreaching the evidence.

Both contributions independently characterize failure modes of LLM-based agents attempting autonomous research tasks, and their findings materially corroborate one another. Contribution A (EXP-Bench) documents quantified failure modes from benchmark evaluation: experimental design misclassification (16.1%), missing implementation components (39.7%), and environment/dependency misconfigurations (29.4%), with an overall 0.5% success rate on complete experiments [A:006, A:002, AQ]. B:012 explicitly notes that "similar errors in setting up libraries and environments were found by researchers working specifically" on this area, further corroborating A's environment/dependency findings. There is no citation link between the papers, and neither explicitly builds on the other's methodology or artifacts. The relationship is one of independent, mutually corroborating empirical findings about the same class of agent failures, making 'supports' the most defensible classification.

Both contributions benchmark LLM-based agents and arrive at materially convergent empirical findings: (1) agents perform reasonably on code-driven/workflow-execution tasks but struggle on more complex, creative, or hypothesis-driven challenges; (2) long-horizon decision making and reasoning quality are key failure modes; (3) scaffold engineering contributes little compared to the base model. Contribution A presents an autonomous AI scientist (Kosmos) as capable of reliably reproducing unpublished findings and generating expert-validated novel discoveries, with 79.4% accuracy and four novel contributions confirmed by domain experts [AQ, A:004, A:008, A:048].
